title: Ten Hikes a Year, Under 10 km: Who the Quechua MH100 Hiking Boots Suit in Kenya
meta_title: Quechua MH100 in Kenya: A Good Budget Boot for 10 km Hikes
meta_description: Quechua MH100 specs, fit, waterproofing and the Kenyan day hikes it suits, from Ngong Hills to Longonot, plus where to buy it in Nairobi.
excerpt: The Quechua MH100 is a light, budget waterproof boot built for day hikes under 10 km. Here are its specs, fit tips and the Kenyan trails it suits, and where it falls short.
content:
Decathlon designs the Quechua MH100 for occasional walkers, and that one label tells Kenyan hikers most of what they need to know. The waterproof mid version suits day hikes of up to about 10 km, such as Ngong Hills, Karura Forest and Mt Longonot in dry weather. It is not built for Aberdares bogs or Mt Kenya summits.

Plenty of people in Nairobi buy a Quechua MH100 as their first proper boot, often because a friend has one or because it costs far less than a leather Lowa. The questions we hear are always the same: is it really waterproof, will it survive Longonot's ash, and what size should I take? Below you will find the published specs, the Kenyan trails the boot handles well, where it runs out of ability, how it compares with the other boots we sell, and how to choose a good second-hand pair.

Quick Facts: Quechua MH100

  • What it is: An entry-level walking boot from Quechua, Decathlon's own hiking brand, made in a waterproof mid-cut version and a low-cut shoe version.
  • Weight: About 440-460 g per boot for the waterproof mid, depending on size and colourway (Decathlon figures).
  • Grip: Rubber outsole with spaced studs of about 4-5 mm, depending on the version.
  • Waterproofing: A breathable membrane lining that Decathlon says keeps feet dry for about 3 hours of walking in wet weather.
  • Designed for: Around 10 hikes a year of 3-4 hours, under 10 km and under 700 m of climbing.
  • Best Kenyan use: Dry-season day hikes near Nairobi; not Elephant Hill mud, Aberdares moorland or Mt Kenya.

What Is the Quechua MH100, and Which Version Should You Look For?

The Quechua MH100 is Decathlon's cheapest dedicated mountain-walking boot, sitting above its NH nature-walking range and below the stiffer MH500. MH stands for mountain hiking, and the 100 marks the entry level of that line.

Several MH100 models carry the same name, which confuses buyers. They share a family look, a rubber outsole with chunky studs and a soft, forgiving feel, but they differ in height and waterproofing. Knowing which one you are holding matters more than the badge on the tongue.

The MH100 Mid waterproof boot

The waterproof Quechua MH100 Mid is the version most Kenyan hikers want. It has a high-cut synthetic upper, a membrane lining, a stone guard across the toes, and locking lace hooks at the ankle that hold the tension between foot and ankle. According to Quechua's own MH100 product page, the upper is a mix of polyester and polyurethane, the midsole runs the full length of the foot, and the insole is removable. The listed weight is 460 g per boot in a UK 8.5.

The MH100 low-cut shoe

The low-cut Quechua MH100 looks like a chunky trainer and comes in waterproof and non-waterproof versions. It is lighter and cooler on hot, dry ridges, but it gives no ankle support and lets in grit and grass seeds over the collar. For a Karura Forest loop it is fine; on a rocky descent from Ol Donyo Sabuk most people are happier in the mid.

Why older pairs can look slightly different

Decathlon updates its ranges every few years, so you will find Quechua MH100 boots with different colourways, lace hooks and stud patterns. Our stock is mostly quality thrifted gear plus some new items, so a pair on our shelf may be an earlier edition. Check the inside label for the model name and size, and treat the figures here as a guide to the family rather than a promise about one specific pair.

Quechua MH100 Specs and What They Mean on Kenyan Trails

On paper the Quechua MH100 is a light, soft, waterproof boot with good grip for its price. The table turns Decathlon's published specs into what you will actually notice on a hike outside Nairobi.

FeatureWhat Decathlon listsWhat it means in Kenya
UpperSynthetic, polyester and polyurethane mix, with a front stone guardDries faster than leather after a wet morning at Ngong; less resistant to sharp lava rock on Longonot
WaterproofingBreathable membrane lining, about 3 hours dry in wet weatherEnough for a short-rains shower; not enough for a full day in Aberdares bog
OutsoleRubber with spaced studs of about 4-5 mmBites into murram and forest mud; spaced studs shed clay better than shallow trainer tread
MidsoleFull-length cushioning (EVA or PU, depending on version)Comfortable from day one; softer underfoot than a stiff trekking boot on loose scree
WeightAbout 440-460 g per bootLight enough that your legs stay fresh over a 4-hour hike
WidthMediumSuits average feet; wide feet may prefer the roomier Keen toe box
Intended useOccasional: about 10 hikes a year, under 10 km, under 700 m of climbingIdeal for monthly day hikes near the city, not for long multi-day treks

Two things stand out. First, the boot is soft. That is why it feels comfortable straight out of the box, and also why it tires your feet on long, rocky descents, because the sole flexes around stones instead of spreading their pressure. Second, the 3-hour waterproof figure is a lab result for walking in wet conditions, not a promise that your feet will stay dry after crossing a stream.

Which Kenyan Trails Suit the Quechua MH100?

The Quechua MH100 is at its best on well-used day-hike trails within about two hours of Nairobi, in the dry months of January-February and June-September. Here is how it matches the hikes people ask us about most.

Ngong Hills ridge

Ngong Hills, about 25 km south-west of Nairobi with a high point of roughly 2,460 m, is close to perfect Quechua MH100 country. The ridge path is grassy and well trodden, the climbs are short and steep, and the full ridge walk sits close to the boot's 10 km design range. The studs grip well on dry grass, and the mid cut keeps out the seed heads that work their way into low shoes. After rain, the black-cotton soil on the lower slopes clogs any tread, so carry a stick to scrape your soles.

Karura, Oloolua and other forest walks

Flat or gently rolling forest trails inside or near the city are well within the Quechua MH100's limits. Karura's murram paths and Oloolua's shaded loops reward a light, cushioned boot more than a heavy leather one. Many people use the low-cut MH100 here, and that works fine in the dry season.

Mt Longonot crater rim

Mt Longonot is the test most Nairobi hikers set themselves, with a climb of roughly 600 m from the gate at about 2,150 m to the 2,776 m summit and around 13.5 km for the full rim loop. That is just beyond the Quechua MH100's design profile, but plenty of hikers finish it happily in this boot. The real issue is the loose volcanic ash: it slides under a soft sole on the steep descent, and fine grit gets past the tongue. Lace firmly, use the locking hooks, and add waterproof leg gaiters if you hate stopping to empty your boots. Our Mt Longonot hike guide covers the route section by section.

Ol Donyo Sabuk

The summit road and footpaths on Ol Donyo Sabuk add up to about 18-20 km return with 700-750 m of climbing, so you are now well past the boot's intended range. It can be done, especially in dry weather, but expect tired soles on the long, stony descent. Read the Ol Donyo Sabuk hike guide before deciding, and if you plan to do several hikes of this length a year, look at a stiffer boot.

Where does the MH100 fall short?

The Quechua MH100 is the wrong tool for the Aberdares and anything high on Mt Kenya. Elephant Hill's bamboo section is ankle-deep mud for hours, Table Mountain and Oldoinyo Lesatima cross waterlogged moorland above 3,400 m, and the membrane will be overwhelmed long before the day ends. On Mt Kenya's summit routes, cold nights near freezing and long scree descents call for a warmer, stiffer, better-supported boot. For those trips, see our guide to waterproof hiking boots in Nairobi.

How Waterproof Is the Quechua MH100 in the Rainy Seasons?

The waterproof Quechua MH100 keeps feet dry through a few hours of wet grass and light rain, which covers most short-rains day hikes. It is not designed for standing water, stream crossings or a whole day of heavy rain.

Decathlon tests the waterproof Quechua MH100 by dipping it to mid-height on a mechanical arm that flexes it like a walking foot, then checks the result with field tests in the rain. The 3-hour figure comes from that process. In Kenyan terms, that means a short-rains morning on Ngong Hills in November, or a damp start in Karura during the April-May long rains, should leave your socks dry. A full day on a muddy Aberdares track will not.

Water also gets in from the top. Once rain runs down your legs or you sink past the collar, no membrane can help, and a membrane boot that is wet inside dries slowly. Rain pants worn over the boot collar, or gaiters, keep water out far better than trousers tucked in. Our rainy season hiking gear guide explains the full set-up.

Socks matter as much as the boot. Cotton holds sweat against the skin, so even a dry boot feels wet after two hours. A pair of merino wool hiking socks stays warmer when damp and dries quicker overnight, which is useful on a two-day camping trip near Naivasha.

How Does the Quechua MH100 Compare With Other Boots We Stock?

Against the other boots we sell, the Quechua MH100 is the lightest and most budget-friendly choice, but it offers less support and durability than the Keen and Lowa options. The right pick depends on how often you hike and how rough the ground is.

  1. Quechua MH100: Soft and light, with a quick break-in. Best for monthly day hikes near Nairobi in dry weather and for people buying their first boots.
  2. Quechua waterproof hiking boot: Similar idea and similar weight class, also from Quechua. A sensible alternative if the MH100 is not in your size that week.
  3. Keen Targhee Mid WP: Nubuck leather upper, a wider toe box and a thick rubber toe cap. Heavier, but tougher on rock and better for wide feet. Our Keen Targhee Mid guide covers it in detail.
  4. Lowa Renegade GTX Mid: A leather boot with a Gore-Tex lining and a firmer sole, built for regular hiking and multi-day treks. The step up for anyone eyeing the Aberdares or Mt Kenya.

A useful rule: if you hike once a month or less and mostly stay below 2,800 m, the Quechua MH100 is enough boot. If you hike every weekend, carry a heavy pack, or have Mt Kenya on your list for next year, spend the extra on a firmer boot now rather than buying twice. How Should the Quechua MH100 Fit?

The Quechua MH100 should feel snug at the heel with a thumb's width of space in front of your longest toe. Decathlon describes it as a medium-width boot, and recommends sizing up if your toes touch the front on descents, as long as the foot stays well held.

Sizing tips before you buy

The current waterproof mid comes in UK 5.5 to UK 12 (EU 39 to 47) on Decathlon's UK site. Labels inside the tongue usually show UK, EU and US sizes, so read the EU number if you are unsure. Try boots in the afternoon, when feet are slightly swollen, and always wear the hiking socks you will use on the trail.

Walk up and down a slope or stairs. On the way up your heel should not lift more than a few millimetres; on the way down your toes should not hit the front. If they do, try half a size larger and lace the locking hooks firmly. People with wide forefeet often find the MH100 a little narrow across the little toe and are happier in a Keen.

Men's and women's versions

Decathlon makes separate men's and women's Quechua MH100 boots. The women's version is built on a narrower last with a lower-volume heel, so a woman with a slim foot is usually better off in the women's model than in a small men's size. Our guide to hiking shoes for women in Nairobi covers fit differences in more detail.

Buying a Second-Hand Quechua MH100: What to Look For

A good thrifted Quechua MH100 can give you seasons of day hikes for a fraction of the new price. Since these are light, soft boots, wear shows quickly, so take two minutes to look over any pair before you pay.

  1. Studs: Look at the forefoot and heel. Rounded edges are fine; studs worn flat under the ball of the foot mean poor grip on Longonot ash.
  2. Midsole: Press your thumb into the side of the sole. Deep, fixed creases or a sole that feels hard and flat suggest the cushioning has packed down.
  3. Sole bond: Bend the boot gently and look along the join between upper and sole, especially at the toe. Any gap will let water in.
  4. Upper and stone guard: Check the flex point above the toes for cracks in the synthetic coating, and make sure the stone guard is not peeling.
  5. Lining: Run your hand inside the heel. Torn lining at the back rubs blisters quickly.
  6. Hooks and laces: The locking hooks should be firm and not bent. Laces are cheap to replace, hooks are not.

Do not expect a used membrane boot to be as waterproof as a new one. Membranes lose some performance over time, and you cannot judge that by looking. If waterproofing matters for your plans, treat the upper with a re-proofing spray as soon as you get home and pair the boots with gaiters in the rainy months. Our post on thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi explains how to judge pre-owned kit more generally.

Common Mistakes With an Entry-Level Boot Like the MH100

Most problems people have with the Quechua MH100 come from asking it to do a job it was never designed for, or from poor care. These are the ones we hear about most often.

Taking it straight to the Aberdares is the big one. A boot built for 10 km in light rain will be soaked through on Elephant Hill, and then people decide the boot is faulty. The second is drying wet boots next to a jiko or campfire. Heat softens the glue and stiffens the synthetic upper, and a sole can start lifting after a single night too close to the flames.

Skipping a short break-in is another. The Quechua MH100 feels soft from day one, but a couple of walks around the estate or Karura still help the insole mould to your foot and show you where a blister might start. Finally, many hikers never replace the factory insole. Decathlon notes that the insole is removable, and a better-supporting insole can make an older pair feel fresher on long descents.

Caring for Your Quechua MH100 Hiking Boots

Quechua MH100 hiking boots need only a brush, warm water and a re-proofing spray. Look after the upper and the glue line, and a light boot like this will cover many more day hikes before the sole wears out.

Decathlon's care advice is simple: let mud dry, then knock it off with a stiff brush; clean marks with a brush and warm water; and dry the boots in the open air. Do not put them in a washing machine or tumble dryer. Take the insoles out after a wet hike and stuff the boots with newspaper, changing it every few hours, and leave them somewhere airy and shaded rather than in hot sun on a Nairobi balcony.

Re-proof the upper twice a year, which in Kenya lines up neatly with the start of the long rains in March and the short rains in October. Spray the outside of a clean, slightly damp boot and let it dry naturally. Store the pair in a ventilated cupboard, away from damp corners and direct light, so the lining does not grow mould between hiking seasons.

Pro Tips for MH100 Owners

  • Lock the hooks: Tighten the lower laces first, then wrap the laces round the locking hooks before the ankle section, so your heel stays put on steep downhills.
  • Scrape early: Clean black-cotton mud off the studs at the first stop, before it dries hard and turns your sole into a slick pad.
  • Match socks to season: Thin merino for hot ridges in February, thicker merino for misty starts in July.
  • Gaiters for ash and rain: Short gaiters keep Longonot grit and Ngong seed heads out, and stop rain running into the collar.
  • Know when to upgrade: If you start hiking every weekend or plan a Mt Kenya climb, move to a firmer boot and keep the Quechua MH100 for forest walks.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Quechua MH100 good enough for Mt Longonot?

The Quechua MH100 is good enough for Mt Longonot in dry weather for most hikers. The waterproof mid grips the ash well on the way up, and its light weight helps on the climb. The steep, loose descent is where a soft sole feels less secure, so lace the locking hooks firmly, take your time, and consider gaiters to keep grit out of your socks.

Can I climb Mt Kenya in Quechua MH100 boots?

Quechua MH100 boots are not a good choice for climbing Mt Kenya to Point Lenana. Decathlon designs them for hikes under 10 km and 700 m of climbing, while a Mt Kenya climb means several long days, cold nights and loose scree. You can wear them around camp or on lower forest sections, but for the summit route choose a stiffer, warmer, fully waterproof trekking boot.

Are MH100 boots fully waterproof?

MH100 boots in the waterproof versions have a breathable membrane lining, and Decathlon says they keep feet dry for about 3 hours of walking in wet weather. That covers short showers and wet grass. They are not meant for stream crossings, deep mud or a whole day of rain, and water will get in over the collar if you sink in. Low-cut non-waterproof MH100 shoes have no membrane.

Do Quechua MH100 boots run true to size?

Quechua MH100 boots are generally close to normal shoe sizing with a medium width, but fit varies between feet and versions. Decathlon suggests going up a size if your toes touch the front on descents, provided the foot stays well held. Try them in the afternoon with hiking socks on, and walk down a slope before deciding which size to buy.

How long do Quechua MH100 boots last?

Quechua MH100 boots last longest when used as intended, for occasional day hikes of a few hours. Lifespan depends on how often you hike, the ground, your weight and how you care for them. Rough lava rock and drying by a fire shorten their life. Brush them clean after each hike, air-dry them away from heat and re-proof them twice a year to keep them going.

Final Thoughts

Light, soft and kind to a first-time hiker's budget, the Quechua MH100 does one job well: day hikes of a few hours on the trails around Nairobi. Use it for Ngong Hills, Karura and a dry-season Longonot with good socks and gaiters. For bamboo mud, moorland and Mt Kenya, step up to a firmer boot.
